secret_exposure_audit.method: Before construction, searched all git-tracked and untracked test/evidence files for hardcoded secret-shaped byte literals (grep for byte-string literals near the word 'key', for os.urandom/secrets.token_bytes usage patterns) and inspected every prior evidence/*.json receipt for literal key bytes.
secret_exposure_audit.finding: No production secret material found anywhere. fabric/tests/test_message_integrity.py (prior mission, untracked) contains one hardcoded dummy byte-string TEST_KEY = b'test-only-integrity-key-not-for-production-use' -- clearly labeled non-production placeholder text, not exploitable material, present only in an untracked test fixture, not in any evidence receipt, log, or serialized wire message. All other prior test files generate key/authkey material via os.urandom() at test run time, never persisted beyond the test process. No evidence/*.json receipt from any prior mission contains literal key bytes -- every 'key'-related field is descriptive prose (design rationale, findings), never a secret value. No STOP condition (BLOCKED_WITH_SECRET_MATERIAL_LEAK) was triggered.
secret_exposure_audit.cli_argument_visibility_note: The prior mission's --integrity-key CLI argument (still supported here as a legacy path) places key material into the process command line, which is visible to other local users via /proc/<pid>/cmdline on POSIX systems in a genuinely multi-user environment -- not exploited in this single-user sandbox, but a real class of exposure for that legacy mechanism. This finding directly motivated THIS mission's own key_store design: --key-store-dir passes only a DIRECTORY PATH (never secret bytes) as a CLI argument; secret material itself is read from a file with 0o600 permissions, never placed on any command line.
secret_exposure_audit.this_missions_own_files: Re-audited after construction: no hardcoded secret byte-string literals in any new file; all secret material in tests is generated via secrets.token_bytes(32) (production-path primitive) or is read back from LocalKeyStore.resolve_key() (never printed, logged, or serialized -- only used locally to call sign_request()).

existing_key_primitives: None found. Searched fabric/interface.py, fabric/loopback/, fabric/tcp/, evidence_envelope/envelope.py, and every production .py file for key/key_id/secret/authkey/credential/token/keystore/keyring/rotation/revoke/revocation/provision/trust/identity/device/peer. The only real matches were: (1) multiprocessing.connection's authkey (connection-establishment secret, not a lifecycle-managed key, already documented as a distinct concern in the prior integrity mission's receipt); (2) evidence_envelope/envelope.py's OWN explicit docstring stating 'there is no revocation or replacement' in its mission-lifecycle machinery; (3) prose mentions of a future 'identity provider' and 'future revocation' as explicitly out-of-scope placeholders. No key_id, keystore, keyring, rotation, or revocation CODE existed anywhere before this mission.
key_model: fabric.interface.LocalKeyStore: metadata (key_id, algorithm, created_at, status, supersedes, revoked_at, reason) is durable JSONL, reusing evidence_envelope.envelope's exact _FileLock/_atomic_write_bytes/_serialize_ledger/LedgerIntegrityError discipline (a fifth application of that pattern, after LineageStore, TrajectoryStore, RequestReplayGuard, and the key-metadata ledger itself). Three lifecycle states only: ACTIVE, RETIRED, REVOKED -- no broader taxonomy introduced.
key_id_contract: integrity_key_id: Optional[str] = None, a new trailing optional field on RemoteCapabilityRequest (same backward-compatible pattern integrity_tag itself used in the prior mission -- no incompatible migration required, confirmed by every prior test file continuing to pass unmodified). The key_id is NOT secret and IS included on the wire (fabric.loopback.wire.capability_request_to_wire()/safe_capability_request_from_wire()); the key MATERIAL never is. integrity_key_id is deliberately NOT part of canonical_request_fields()'s HMAC-covered input -- an attacker swapping key_id without possessing any secret cannot produce a combination (new key_id, old tag) that verify_request_integrity() accepts against the newly-named key's actual secret, so omitting it from the signed content is safe by construction, not an oversight.
generation_primitive: secrets.token_bytes(32) (stdlib, cryptographically secure) -- never derived from a username, device name, timestamp, or password; no KDF invented. key_bytes may be supplied explicitly to provision_key() ONLY for deterministic unit testing of the store's own logic; every end-to-end/transport test uses store-generated random material.
storage_model: Two-part LOCAL filesystem storage under one root directory: (1) key_metadata.jsonl + key_metadata.lock -- non-secret lifecycle ledger, world-readable-by-default (same as LineageStore's own ledger; contains no secret bytes so this is not a new exposure). (2) secrets/<key_id>.secret -- ONE PLAIN FILE PER KEY, written atomically via envelope._atomic_write_bytes then chmod'd 0o600 immediately after; the containing secrets/ directory is chmod'd 0o700 at store construction (best-effort, POSIX only).
storage_security_limitations: Plaintext key material at rest, protected ONLY by POSIX file permission bits -- NOT an OS keychain/keyring, NOT a hardware security module or secure enclave, NOT encrypted at rest. Anyone with filesystem read access as the same user (or root) can read a secret file directly. chmod is a no-op (best-effort, silently ignored) on platforms without POSIX permission bits (e.g. Windows), matching the exact same documented limitation evidence_envelope.envelope._FileLock already carries for its own POSIX-only fcntl locking. This is explicitly a LOCAL PROOF primitive, never claimed as production key management.
active_key_result: CAP_COMPLETED, executes exactly once (proven in-process, loopback subprocess, and TCP subprocess; loopback/TCP tests additionally assert the secret bytes and their hex encoding are absent from the serialized wire request).
unknown_key_result: CAP_FAILED, zero execution (a syntactically valid but never-provisioned key_id) -- proven in-process and over both transports.
malformed_key_result: CAP_FAILED, zero execution (a key_id that fails envelope.validate_mission_id's format contract, and separately, a request with integrity_key_id entirely absent) -- proven in-process.
revoked_key_result: CAP_FAILED, zero execution, even though the HMAC is mathematically correct under the key's own (still known-to-the-test) secret bytes -- proven in-process, over both transports, and confirmed to survive a real second-subprocess restart (revoke before restart, still rejected after).
rotation_result: HARD CUTOVER, not a bounded compatibility window (an explicit, documented design decision, not a silent default): provision_key(supersedes=k1) atomically marks k1 RETIRED and k2 ACTIVE under one lock. A request signed with k2 (the new key) after rotation is accepted; the SAME logical request signed with k1 (the old key) before rotation, if delivered after rotation completes, is rejected -- proven in-process and over both real transports. RETIRED and REVOKED remain independently observable via status_of() and the metadata ledger even though both currently produce the identical fail-closed execution outcome (documented as a deliberate simplification, not an oversight -- see limitations).
process_restart_result: PROVEN with a REAL second OS subprocess for both transports (not simulated in-process only, though in-process proxies are also included for completeness): an ACTIVE key provisioned before a server subprocess starts remains usable by a server subprocess reading the same --key-store-dir; a key revoked between two subprocess lifetimes remains REVOKED (and its secret unresolvable) when a second, genuinely separate subprocess is started against the identical directory.
authority_interaction: Proven orthogonal in every direction required by Section 13: ACTIVE key + expired authority -> CAP_UNAUTHORIZED (not CAP_FAILED -- integrity passed, a DIFFERENT gate denied); ACTIVE key + invalid/empty authority -> zero execution via the existing, unmodified authority_permits() gate; REVOKED key + otherwise-valid authority -> CAP_FAILED, zero execution, before authority is ever evaluated. Key acceptance and execution authority remain two separate, non-substitutable gates.
replay_interaction: A genuinely valid, unmutated resend is still recognized and suppressed (CAP_DUPLICATE_COMPLETED) when key_store and replay_guard are configured together (TestValidDuplicateWithKeyStorePreservesReplaySemantics). The harder case (Section 12/matrix item 14): a request that completed successfully while its key was ACTIVE, replayed IDENTICALLY (same bytes, same tag) after that key is later REVOKED, is rejected as CAP_FAILED -- NOT returned as CAP_DUPLICATE_COMPLETED -- because integrity/key-resolution is verified on EVERY delivery, not only the first, and now runs strictly before replay_guard is ever consulted. This is a deliberate, documented policy choice: 'historical disposition retrieval' still requires the presented message to currently verify under a currently-ACTIVE key; a revoked key can retroactively make even an already-completed request's exact replay unrecoverable through this path. Zero additional execution either way -- the distinction is only in which rejection reason is returned.
integrity_interaction: key_store is a NEW, independent precedence branch in process_remote_capability_request(): when supplied it takes precedence over the prior mission's raw integrity_key parameter, which remains fully functional and unmodified for backward compatibility (every prior integrity test, unedited, still passes). The two mechanisms are mutually exclusive per call, never combined.
tcp_allowlist_observation: Re-examined per Section 20: fabric/tcp/pc_node_server.py's pre-existing capability_id allowlist check still sits outside process_remote_capability_request(), unchanged by this mission. This mission's own transport tests deliberately avoided that specific field (using artifact_id/key_id mutations instead, as the prior mission's tests already did for the analogous integrity case), so no NEW instance of the observation was produced. Classification: (A) only equivalent fail-closed behavior -- both the TCP allowlist's CAP_UNSUPPORTED and this mission's CAP_FAILED are zero-execution outcomes; no information leak or trust-boundary violation was found (no distinguishable capability was gained by an attacker from knowing which rejection reason came back, since both require the same fail-closed non-execution). Recorded as a candidate defect for a future consistency pass, not repaired here, per explicit instruction not to expand scope.

counterevidence: None found against the core claim. Confirmed one deliberate design simplification rather than a bug: RETIRED and REVOKED currently share identical fail-closed execution behavior (resolve_key() returns None for both), distinguished only in the audit-layer metadata, not in runtime behavior -- explicitly documented as a choice, not discovered as a defect.
limitations: No bounded compatibility window for rotation: a message signed with the immediately-previous key and delivered even microseconds after rotation is rejected. A future microphase could add a time-boxed grace period for RETIRED specifically (never for REVOKED) if operational experience shows hard cutover is too strict for real phone/PC clock skew and delivery latency.

Plaintext-at-rest key storage (POSIX file permissions only) -- explicitly not an OS keychain, HSM, or encrypted store. Recorded, not solved, per this mission's own storage-security-limitations requirement.

No key distribution/pairing mechanism: this mission proves a key can be generated, persisted, resolved, rotated, and revoked LOCALLY. How a real phone and a real PC would ever come to share the SAME secret bytes in the first place (out-of-band pairing, QR code, manual entry, or otherwise) is entirely unaddressed and is the natural next prerequisite before any physical-device integrity work.

TCP-allowlist ordering observation (Section 20) re-examined, not repaired -- classified as equivalent fail-closed behavior across both rejection paths, not a new defect, per the explicit instruction not to expand scope to repair it.

active_key_for_signing() assumes at most one 'current' ACTIVE key per rotation chain is meaningful for a sender; a store with multiple, UNRELATED ACTIVE keys (no supersedes chain linking them) will return only the most-recently-provisioned one to a naive caller -- adequate for this mission's local single-key-lineage proof, not evaluated for a multi-key concurrent-active scenario.
key_management_gap: Key distribution/pairing between two real, physically separate devices remains entirely unaddressed -- named as the explicit prerequisite before physical Android<->PC key-provisioning work.
peer_identity_gap: Unaddressed by design (explicit prohibition this mission). A key_id names a KEY; it carries no semantic identity (no PHONE_JAMES/PC_JAMES/TRUSTED_DEVICE-style binding exists anywhere in this store).
transport_encryption_gap: Unaddressed (out of scope, unchanged from the prior mission). All wire traffic, including the non-secret key_id and integrity_tag, remains plaintext.
crash_window_b_status: Unchanged, still open, not addressed per explicit instruction: a receiver crash between successful provider.invoke() and durable disposition persistence remains an unresolved risk, orthogonal to key lifecycle.

resulting_capability_claim.claim: LOCAL_INTEGRITY_KEY_LIFECYCLE_PROVEN -- ForgeWorld can locally generate (secrets.token_bytes), provision (durable ACTIVE metadata + a 0o600 secret file), identify (a non-secret key_id, safely carried on the wire), persist (JSONL metadata ledger surviving a real process restart), resolve (fail-closed on unknown/malformed/retired/revoked key_id), rotate (a documented hard-cutover policy, old key immediately unusable, new key immediately usable), and revoke (durably distinct from retirement in the audit trail, immediately fail-closed in execution) message-integrity keys, entirely locally, without the secret key material ever being serialized into a RemoteCapabilityRequest, a wire message, a RemoteCapabilityResult, a FabricReceipt, or a RequestReplayGuard disposition record.
